newsitem.title: UK: Israel's Weizman appeals for calm in Middle East.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Weizman appeals for calm in Middle East.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman said on Wednesday the Middle East peace process was still on track and appealed for Palestinian calm over Israeli construction plans for Arab East Jerusalem.

"I am very optimistic about the future with the ups and downs like you have today -- but we will overcome it," he told reporters after meeting Prime Minister John Major on the first visit to Britain by an Israeli head of state.
Palestinian and Israeli leftists have warned that a plan to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem would ignite Arab fury.
Calling for calm as tension rose in Israel, he said: "We don't want to go back to bombs and bombing."

The plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a hill taken by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War has sparked fears that violence could erupt again. Sixty-one Arabs and 15 Israelis were killed in clashes after hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided last September to open an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
Weizman insisted the peace process would continue telling reporters: "All parties concerned, including ourselves, would be stupid and crazy...to damage it."

"I recommend to the Palestinian authorities and all parties that are worried that this should not be a stumbling block. We will overcome it and see Jerusalem blooming and building both for Arabs and Jews at the same time," he said.

The U.N. Security Council has expressed concern over the Israeli settlement plans and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat has said they were aimed at making demographic changes that went against the peace process.
Britain's Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind added his voice to the disquiet.
"I am extremely disturbed to hear that the Israeli government have decided to go ahead with building a settlement at Har Homa," Rifkind said in a statement.

"We have urged the Israeli government not to proceed with these plans. They can only detract from the positive atmosphere created by the Hebron agreement and undermine the establishment of trust vital to the succesful negotiation of final status issues with the Palestinians," he said.

At his press conference, Weizman ruled out granting clemency to nuclear technician Mordechai Vanunu, who has spent 10 years in solitary confinement after being jailed for giving details of Israel's nuclear programme to the London Sunday Times.
"I don't think he deserves clemency. Vanunu is a spy who gave secrets...He was a man who was a traitor to his country," he said.

Weizman, a former fighter pilot with Britain's Royal Air Force, invited Queen Elizabeth to visit Israel. Officials said she would be happy to do so "at a mutually convenient time" but indicated the trip was not imminent.
The queen, watched by Weizman, unveiled a monument to Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews from Nazi concentration camps in World War Two.

The ceremony to honour "the epitome of good over evil" was also attended by U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, whose wife is a niece of Wallenberg, as well as five people who survived the Holocaust thanks to Wallenberg's bravery.
